value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
variable_description: The day a resident took up a place of a particular type inside a residential aged care home. The AIHW data dictionary for this collection defines the element as one that "Identifies the date a person was admitted into care", and warns that "Moving from one type of place to another within the same service/facility will involve two records with differing admission dates". That is why rac_episode also carries ENTRY_DATE and EXIT_DATE: those two bracket a continuous stay in the service, while ADMISSION_DATE and DISCHARGE_DATE bracket a stay in one type of place within it. Read with ADMISSION_TYPE, it dates the start of a permanent stay or of a respite stay.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
value_definition: A calendar date, held in the source system as DD/MM/YYYY. It is a claiming date drawn from the residential care payment system rather than a clinical record, so it is the day from which subsidy was payable for the place.
limitation: A second admission date for the same person and home is not proof of a second stay: a resident who converts from a respite place to a permanent place inside the same home gets a fresh row with no gap in care. The column also carries no waiting time, because the aged care assessment that approved the person sits on a different table with its own approval dates.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary documents admission_date as a common data element of this collection, gives its definition and data domain, and explains the place-type behaviour that produces multiple admission rows for one continuous stay.
evidence_quote: Moving from one type of place to another within the same service/facility will involve two records with differing admission dates.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's wording, 'Date of admission of recipient to a place of a particular type in a service facility', and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both its value definition and its limitation.

value_domain: residential aged care admission type (permanent or respite)
value_source: AIHW GEN Aged Care Data, Glossary
variable_description: Whether the residential stay starting on this row was a permanent placement or a short respite stay. The AIHW GEN glossary draws the same line: "Admission to residential care can be long-term and on an ongoing basis (permanent residential care) or short-term on a planned or emergency basis (residential respite care)." The distinction governs almost everything else about the row, because respite stays are capped in days and permanent stays are not, and because the two are funded and means tested differently. The AIHW records that respite care is still offered at high and low care levels, while that split was removed for permanent care from 1 July 2014.
description_source: AIHW GEN Aged Care Data, Glossary
value_definition: A short text label separating permanent residential care from residential respite care. It restates the care type the place was approved for, which is the same distinction the Australian Government uses to set the subsidy and the fee rules for the stay.
limitation: It does not show a respite stay turning into a permanent one. A person who converts is given a separate row with its own admission date, so following one person needs the rows ordered rather than this column read alone. Nor does the column carry any respite day balance, so it cannot say whether a stay fell inside the 63 days of respite a person is entitled to in a financial year.
rationale: The GEN glossary, published by the AIHW alongside this data holding, defines residential care in exactly the permanent-or-respite terms the column encodes, and the NACDC data dictionary describes the same split in its account of the residential aged care collection.
evidence_quote: Admission to residential care can be long-term and on an ongoing basis (permanent residential care) or short-term on a planned or emergency basis (residential respite care).
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried only the custodian's phrasing and the generic sentence saying no finite value list is published, printed twice.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
variable_description: The day a resident stopped occupying a place of a particular type in a residential aged care home. The AIHW data dictionary defines the element as "The date on which a person left an aged care service", and notes that it is "Used to calculate periods of care" and that moving between place types inside one home produces "two records with differing discharge dates". Pair it with ADMISSION_DATE on the same row for the length of that placement, and with EXIT_REASON for where the person went.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
value_definition: A calendar date in DD/MM/YYYY in the source system. It comes from the residential care payment system, so it marks the last day subsidy was claimed for the place rather than a separately recorded departure.
limitation: An empty discharge date means the person was still in the place when the extract was taken, not that the placement never ended, so any completed-stay analysis silently drops long current residents and shortens average length of stay. The date also gives no destination on its own: a discharge to hospital, to another home and to death all look the same until EXIT_REASON is read.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary documents discharge_date as a common data element of this collection, with its definition, its DD/MM/YYYY domain and the guidance that place-type moves generate paired discharge records.
evidence_quote: The date on which a person left an aged care service.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's wording and used one generic sentence for both the value definition and the limitation.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
variable_description: The day an aged care assessment team decision took effect, opening the person's eligibility for the care named on the same row. The AIHW data dictionary defines the paired element as "The effective start date of approval for care (ACAP/ACCR) or funding (ACFI/RCS), and the effective end date for same". It qualifies CARE_APPROVAL_TYPE and CARE_APPROVAL_LEVEL, which say what was approved, and sits before any entry date in hcp_episode, since approval and entry are separate steps handled by different parties.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
value_definition: A calendar date in DD/MM/YYYY in the source system, taken from the assessment record rather than from a service provider. It dates the legal effect of the approval, which can differ from the day the assessment was conducted.
limitation: Approval is not care. The AIHW notes that the assessment programme only grants approval, that providers handle entry, and that a varying amount of time passes in between, so this date is a poor proxy for when support began and a gap to ENTRY_DATE measures queueing rather than need.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary documents assessment_start_date and assessment_end_date as a single common data element covering the effective dates of an approval for care, which is what the home care assessment table holds.
evidence_quote: The effective start date of approval for care (ACAP/ACCR) or funding (ACFI/RCS), and the effective end date for same.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'The date the approval decision started.' and carried the generic no-value-list sentence in both the value definition and the limitation.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
variable_description: The day an aged care assessment team decision stopped having effect, closing the eligibility that APPROVAL_START_DATE opened. The AIHW data dictionary covers both dates in one element, "The effective start date of approval for care (ACAP/ACCR) or funding (ACFI/RCS), and the effective end date for same". Most approvals end because a later reassessment replaced them rather than because the person stopped needing care, so the two dates together describe how long one particular decision stood.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
value_definition: A calendar date in DD/MM/YYYY in the source system. The AIHW notes for the related effective-date element that an end date is frequently open-ended, and an open value marks a record that was still active.
limitation: A closed approval is not evidence that care ended or that the person was found ineligible. It is also not a waiting time: a person can hold a live approval for years without entering care, so the interval between the two approval dates measures the life of a decision, not the length of any service episode.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary documents the effective start and end dates of approval for care as one common data element, and separately notes that end dates are commonly left open while a record is active.
evidence_quote: End date is frequently open-ended and indicates the record is active.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'The date the approval decision ended.' and printed the same generic sentence as both value definition and limitation.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
variable_description: The band of care an assessment approved the person for, which for home care is one of the four package levels. The AIHW data dictionary defines care level as "The level of care a person receives through an aged care program" or "The level of care assigned to an aged care place", and records that home care has Level 1 to Level 4, that the earlier packages CACP, EACH and EACHD map onto Level 2 and Level 4 from July 2013, and that respite residential care keeps a high and low split. It qualifies CARE_APPROVAL_TYPE, which names the programme, and should be read against ENTRY_CARE_LEVEL in hcp_episode, which is what the person actually took up.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
value_definition: A short text label naming a level rather than an amount. Levels are funding bands: the Australian Government pays a different daily subsidy at each one, so the label is a rung on a payment scale set by the assessment, not a score.
limitation: An approval at a level does not mean a package at that level was received. People commonly enter on a lower level while waiting for the one they were approved for, which is why ENTRY_CARE_LEVEL exists and why comparing the two is the only way to see the shortfall. The column also carries no assessed need behind the band, so two people approved at Level 3 can differ widely.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary carries care level as a data concept of this collection, with the definition and the full programme-by-programme account of what the levels are in home care, in the earlier package programmes and in respite residential care.
evidence_quote: The level of care a person receives through an aged care program.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'The level of care the person is approved to receive as represented by text.' and used the generic no-value-list sentence for both the definition and the limitation.

value_domain: aged care programme approved after assessment
value_source: AIHW METEOR data element 807747, 'Aged care assessment-approved program, code N[N]'
variable_description: The aged care programme an assessment cleared the person to use. AIHW METEOR defines the matching national element as "The type of aged care program(s) a person has been approved to receive on the basis of an aged care assessment, as represented by a code", with a code list separating permanent residential aged care, residential respite, transition care and home support. CARE_APPROVAL_LEVEL beside it says at what level, and the approval dates on the same row say when the decision applied. A person can hold approvals for more than one programme at once, so a row is a decision rather than a pathway.
description_source: AIHW METEOR data element 807747, 'Aged care assessment-approved program, code N[N]'
value_definition: A short text label naming a programme. The national classification behind it runs 1 residential aged care (permanent), 2 residential aged care (respite), 4 Transition Care Program, 6 Support at Home, 7 Commonwealth Home Support Programme, 10 other, 11 none, with 97 to 99 for not applicable, unknown and not stated.
limitation: It cannot be used to count the people a programme serves. Approval is granted well before entry and many approvals are never taken up, so counting approvals overstates use. It also cannot be used to find home support clients, because the AIHW records that approval under the assessment programme is not required to access that programme and those clients may carry no approval row at all.
rationale: METEOR publishes the national data element for the programme approved on the basis of an aged care assessment, which is the concept this column encodes, with the definition and the code list. The NACDC data dictionary separately confirms that home support access does not require an assessment programme approval.
evidence_quote: The type of aged care program(s) a person has been approved to receive on the basis of an aged care assessment, as represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'The type of care the person is approved to receive as represented by text.' with the generic no-value-list sentence in both the definition and the limitation.

value_source: Australian Government Department of Veterans' Affairs, Veteran Card
variable_description: Whether the person held a Department of Veterans' Affairs treatment card when the aged care assessment was done, as the assessor recorded it. DVA publishes three cards: the "Veteran Card - All Conditions (VCAC) (colloquially known as the Veteran Gold Card) gives access to treatment for all medical conditions", the Specific Conditions or White Card covers accepted service-related conditions, and the Pharmaceuticals Only or Orange Card gives concessions on medicines. It matters at assessment because a card holder may be routed to DVA-funded support such as Veterans' Home Care instead of, or alongside, the aged care programme being assessed.
description_source: Australian Government Department of Veterans' Affairs, Veteran Card
value_definition: A short text label naming the card, or its absence. The categories come from DVA's own card scheme rather than from an aged care classification, so the same labels appear in other DVA-linked collections.
limitation: A card is a treatment entitlement, not a service record, so it does not show that any DVA-funded care was used and none of that care appears in this dataset. It is also not a veteran flag: a former member with no accepted condition and no qualifying service holds no card, and the value is fixed at the date of the assessment, so a card granted later never appears on the row.
rationale: DVA publishes the three Veteran Card types and what each entitles the holder to, which is the classification this column records at the point of aged care assessment.
evidence_quote: Veteran Card - All Conditions (VCAC) (colloquially known as the Veteran Gold Card) gives access to treatment for all medical conditions.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'Whether the person holds a dva entitlement as represented by text.' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both value definition and limitation.

value_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, My Aged Care - Application for Emergency Residential Care or Residential Respite Care Form
variable_description: The day an approval for emergency entry to residential care or residential respite care took effect. Emergency approval is the pathway used when someone has to enter care before an assessment can be completed, and the department's own form for it is submitted by the provider after the fact, within five business days after the day care starts. The AIHW GEN glossary describes residential respite as available on either a planned or an emergency basis, and this column is the date stamp on the second of those. It is populated only for assessments that used the emergency pathway, so most rows are empty.
description_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, My Aged Care - Application for Emergency Residential Care or Residential Respite Care Form
value_definition: A calendar date. It belongs to the approval decision rather than to any service record, so it marks when the emergency authorisation began to apply.
limitation: An empty value is the ordinary planned pathway rather than a gap in the data, so treating blanks as missing will misstate how common emergency entry is. Because the paperwork follows the care, the date can also fall after the person was already in the home, which makes it unusable as an entry date.
rationale: The department publishes the emergency residential care and residential respite application, confirming that emergency approval is a distinct pathway granted around the start of care, and the GEN glossary confirms residential respite runs on a planned or emergency basis. Neither publishes a data element definition for this exact column, so the description is assembled rather than quoted.
evidence_quote: Approved providers should submit this form it to the relevant assessment organisation within 5 business days after the day care starts.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Date that approval for emergency care started' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence as both the value definition and the limitation.

value_source: AIHW METEOR data element 807741, 'Aged care assessment-assessment setting, code N[N]'
variable_description: Where the assessment team first met the person face to face, which is usually where the person was living or being treated at the time. The closest published national element, AIHW METEOR's aged care assessment setting, defines the concept as "The setting in which an aged care assessment took place, as represented by a code" and separates the person's home, a carer's home, another community setting, a residential care home, private and public hospitals, other inpatient settings and clinics. The setting is worth reading as a route into care rather than as a location: a hospital contact usually means a discharge-driven assessment, while a home contact usually means a community-initiated one.
description_source: AIHW METEOR data element 807741, 'Aged care assessment-assessment setting, code N[N]'
value_definition: A short text label naming a setting. The national classification behind it groups settings into home and community, residential care, hospital inpatient and clinical, with separate residual codes for other, not applicable, unknown and not stated.
limitation: It is not the person's address or usual accommodation. Someone assessed in a public hospital may live alone at home and return there, so using this column as a living situation will misclassify every hospital-initiated assessment. It also records one contact only, so it says nothing about where later contacts or the reassessment took place.
rationale: METEOR publishes the national aged care assessment setting element with the definition and its full code list, which is the classification this column belongs to. The column names the first face-to-face contact specifically, and no separately published element with that exact wording could be verified, so the description is written rather than quoted.
evidence_quote: The setting in which an aged care assessment took place, as represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's sentence about first face-to-face contact and gave the generic no-value-list sentence as both value definition and limitation.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
variable_description: The month of the year in which the care recipient was born, kept without the day. The aged care source systems hold a full date of birth, which the AIHW records as the basis for calculating age and as one of the fields used with sex and letters of name for statistical record linkage; what reaches this table is that date reduced to a month and a year so the person cannot be identified from it. Paired with BIRTH_YEAR it pins age to within a month at any admission, discharge or assessment date on the other tables.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
value_definition: An integer from 1 to 12, or the month written out, depending on the extract. It carries no year of its own and is meaningless without BIRTH_YEAR beside it.
limitation: It cannot reproduce a person's exact age, so an age at admission built from it can be wrong by up to about thirty days, which matters at the aged care eligibility ages of 50 and 65. Nor can it be used to confirm identity against another collection holding a full date of birth, since the day of the month is gone.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary documents date of birth as a common data element of this collection, gives its use in age calculation and record linkage, and lists the tables it appears on. The reduction to month and year is a de-identification step rather than a published element, so the description is written rather than quoted.
evidence_quote: The date on which a person was born.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Person's month of birth.' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence twice, once as the definition and once as the limitation.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
variable_description: The year the care recipient was born, the coarser half of the reduced date of birth held on this table. The AIHW records that age in this data holding is normally calculated at 30 June, or at the date of admission to or separation from a programme, so this column is the input to almost every age figure published from the collection. It is also what makes the aged care target population reportable, since eligibility turns on being 65 or over, or 50 or over for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people and people who are homeless or at risk of homelessness.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
value_definition: A four-digit year. Combined with BIRTH_MONTH it gives a birth date accurate to the month; on its own it gives an age accurate only to a year.
limitation: An age built from the year alone will disagree with published AIHW age distributions for everyone whose birthday falls after the reference date, because the AIHW ages people at 30 June rather than at 1 January. The column also carries no death information, so it cannot be used to work out whether an older recipient is still alive.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary documents date of birth as a common data element and defines the age concept built from it, including the 30 June reference point used in the AIHW's own reporting from this holding.
evidence_quote: The person's age, calculated from their date of birth.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Year of birth' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence as both the value definition and the limitation.

value_domain: Standard Australian Classification of Countries (SACC) country code
value_source: AIHW METEOR data element 659454, 'Person-country of birth, code (SACC 2016) NNNN'
variable_description: Where the care recipient was born, held as an ABS country code. AIHW METEOR defines the national element as "The country in which the person was born, as represented by a code", coded to the Standard Australian Classification of Countries; the AIHW records that in this data holding the values in use run from 1101 to 9999 and that the field is used to estimate cultural and linguistic diversity. COUNTRY_OF_BIRTH_DESC on the same row is the label for this code. The custodian wording attached to the field mentions a student, which is carried over from an unrelated education collection and does not describe who is in this table.
description_source: AIHW METEOR data element 659454, 'Person-country of birth, code (SACC 2016) NNNN'
value_definition: A four-digit numeric code from the Standard Australian Classification of Countries, which the ABS builds as a three-level hierarchy of major group, minor group and country. Each country is one unit regardless of its internal divisions, so a code identifies a country rather than a region within one.
limitation: Country of birth is not ancestry, citizenship or language, and reading it as any of those will misplace people born abroad to Australian parents and Australian-born children of migrants alike. It also drives a cruder derived measure than it looks: the AIHW treats only Australia, the United Kingdom, Ireland, the United States, Canada and South Africa as English-speaking countries, so a New Zealand-born recipient falls into the non-English-speaking background group.
rationale: METEOR publishes the national country of birth element and its SACC value domain, and the NACDC data dictionary confirms this holding codes country of birth to SACC, gives the range of values in use and sets out the English-speaking country list behind its derived diversity measure.
evidence_quote: The country in which the person was born, as represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the mismatched custodian wording 'Student's country of birth (code).' and the generic no-value-list sentence in both the definition and the limitation.

value_domain: Standard Australian Classification of Countries (SACC) country name
value_source: AIHW METEOR data element 659454, 'Person-country of birth, code (SACC 2016) NNNN'
variable_description: The country name that goes with COUNTRY_OF_BIRTH_CODE on the same row, saved so a table can be read without a lookup. It labels the element AIHW METEOR defines as "The country in which the person was born, as represented by a code", drawn from the ABS Standard Australian Classification of Countries. Use the code for grouping and this column for display: the label is the more fragile of the pair.
description_source: AIHW METEOR data element 659454, 'Person-country of birth, code (SACC 2016) NNNN'
value_definition: A country name written out, taken from the SACC edition in force when the record was coded. Names sit at the four-digit country level of the classification rather than at the major or minor group level.

Country names change between SACC editions and successor states appear and disappear, so grouping on the label will split one country across spellings and merge nothing that was renamed. Two rows agreeing on the label may also disagree on the code, and the code is the value the AIHW reports from.
rationale: METEOR publishes the national country of birth element and its SACC value domain, in which the label and the four-digit code are two representations of the same classification unit.
evidence_quote: The country in which the person was born, as represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's sentence and used one generic sentence as both value definition and limitation.

value_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Veterans' supplement for aged care
variable_description: The day from which the Department of Veterans' Affairs accepts that a veteran's mental health condition is related to their service, which is the trigger for the veterans' supplement in aged care. The department sets the test plainly: to be eligible a person must "be a veteran" and "have a mental health condition that the Department of Veterans' Affairs (DVA) accepts is related to their service". DVA_VETERAN_SUPP_FLAG on the same row says whether the supplement applied at all; this column dates the condition behind it, and payment starts on the day the person entered care or became eligible, whichever is later.
description_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Veterans' supplement for aged care
value_definition: A calendar date. It marks an administrative acceptance by DVA rather than an event recorded by an aged care provider, and it reaches this collection through a data match between DVA and Services Australia.
limitation: It is not a date of onset, of first symptom or of diagnosis, so it cannot be used to study when veterans became unwell. The row also names no condition: the department states that the eligibility information released to the provider and Services Australia does not include information about the person's mental health condition.
rationale: The department publishes the eligibility rule for the veterans' supplement in aged care, the DVA and Services Australia matching that establishes it, and the limit on what condition information is released, which together define what this date can and cannot stand for.
evidence_quote: have a mental health condition that the Department of Veterans' Affairs (DVA) accepts is related to their service
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's long sentence about the supplement and gave the generic no-value-list sentence as both the value definition and the limitation.

value_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Veterans' supplement for aged care
variable_description: Whether the care recipient attracted the veterans' supplement, an extra daily payment to their aged care provider. The department describes it as a supplement that "helps with the cost of caring for veterans with a mental health condition related to their service", paid automatically to residential aged care and in-home care providers once the person agrees to release their eligibility information. DVA_MENTAL_HEALTH_DATE on the same row dates the accepted condition behind the flag. In practice the column identifies a narrow group: veterans with a DVA-accepted service-related mental health condition who were in subsidised aged care.
description_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Veterans' supplement for aged care
value_definition: A yes or no indicator against the person rather than against an episode. The underlying payment is a flat daily rate, set at 7.99 dollars a day in residential aged care from 1 July 2024 and scaled by home care package level in home care.

A veteran with no accepted service-related mental health condition is not marked, and a person with such a condition who never entered subsidised aged care never appears, so the column cannot be used to count veterans in this population. Because the money goes to the provider, it also says nothing about what care the person actually received.
rationale: The department publishes what the veterans' supplement is for, who is eligible, how payment is triggered and which care types it applies to, and the published schedule of subsidies and supplements gives the rates that sit behind the flag.
evidence_quote: This supplement helps with the cost of caring for veterans with a mental health condition related to their service.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Whether the person is eligible for the veterans' supplement for aged care.' with the generic no-value-list sentence repeated as both definition and limitation.

Because the flag beside it, HCP_DEMENTIA_SUPP_FLAG, is an ever-received marker, this column is the earliest date anywhere behind that history rather than a date tied to any one episode.

Only people who received the home care supplement can have a date here, so people with dementia in residential care, in home support or with no subsidised care at all are blank and cannot be told apart from people without the condition. The date also reflects when the diagnosis was recorded for claiming, which can be well after the condition began.
rationale: The department publishes the dementia and cognition supplement as a home care payment scaled by package level, which establishes what population can carry a value in this column and why the record exists at all. No published element definition for this specific date could be verified, so the description is assembled.

value_source: AIHW METEOR data element 291045, 'Person-marital status, code N'
variable_description: The care recipient's relationship status as recorded at the aged care assessment, held as a code. AIHW METEOR defines the national element as "A person's current relationship status in terms of a couple relationship or, for those not in a couple relationship, the existence of a current or previous registered marriage, as represented by a code". MARITAL_STATUS_DESC on the same row is the label. In aged care the field carries weight beyond demography, because a partner is often the informal carer whose availability decides whether someone can stay at home.
description_source: AIHW METEOR data element 291045, 'Person-marital status, code N'
value_definition: A single-digit code. The national classification runs 1 never married, 2 widowed, 3 divorced, 4 separated, 5 married including de facto, and 6 not stated or inadequately described.
limitation: The value is fixed at the assessment and never revised, so a person widowed after their assessment still shows as married on this table, which is a common event in this population. The classification also folds registered marriage and de facto partnering into one value, so it cannot be used to identify legal spouses for estate or means-testing questions.
rationale: METEOR publishes the national marital status element used across health and community services collections, with the definition and the full code list this column follows.
evidence_quote: A person's current relationship status in terms of a couple relationship or, for those not in a couple relationship, the existence of a current or previous registered marriage, as represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Marital status of the recipient (at time of assessment)' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence as both value definition and limitation.

value_source: AIHW METEOR data element 291045, 'Person-marital status, code N'
variable_description: The written label for MARITAL_STATUS_CODE on the same row, so the table reads without a lookup. It labels the national element AIHW METEOR defines as "A person's current relationship status in terms of a couple relationship or, for those not in a couple relationship, the existence of a current or previous registered marriage, as represented by a code". Group on the code and display this column, since the labels are what change between collections while the codes do not.
description_source: AIHW METEOR data element 291045, 'Person-marital status, code N'
value_definition: Short text: never married, widowed, divorced, separated, married including de facto, or a not stated value. The married label covers registered and de facto relationships together, which is the classification's own choice rather than a coding shortcut.
limitation: Reading the label alone hides how much it merges. Married here includes de facto, and separated is a self-reported state with no legal test, so a count of married recipients built from this text answers a different question from a count of legally married ones. The wording also varies between the source systems this collection draws on, so exact string matching across years is unsafe.
rationale: METEOR publishes the national marital status element with the definition and the code and label pairs that this column displays.
evidence_quote: A person's current relationship status in terms of a couple relationship or, for those not in a couple relationship, the existence of a current or previous registered marriage, as represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's circular wording, 'Marital status code of person as represented by text.', and one generic sentence used twice.

value_domain: Australian Standard Classification of Languages (ASCL) language code
value_source: AIHW METEOR data element 659407, 'Person-preferred language, code (ASCL 2016) N[NNN]'
variable_description: The language the care recipient would rather be spoken to in, held as an ABS language code. AIHW METEOR defines the national element as "The language (including sign language) most preferred by the person for communication, as represented by a code", and notes that this "may be a language other than English even where the person can speak fluent English". The AIHW records preferred language as a separate element from main language spoken at home and as one available only through the recipient table, so it is the aged care system's own record of communication need rather than a household characteristic.
description_source: AIHW METEOR data element 659407, 'Person-preferred language, code (ASCL 2016) N[NNN]'
value_definition: A numeric code of up to four digits from the Australian Standard Classification of Languages, built as a three-level hierarchy: one digit for a broad group, two or three for a narrow group and four for a specific language. Sign languages are inside the classification, not outside it.
limitation: It records a preference, not proficiency, so it cannot be used to identify people who need an interpreter: a fluent English speaker may still prefer another language, and someone with little English may be recorded as preferring it. It also holds one language where many older migrants use several, and it is not the same field as main language spoken at home, which is collected separately and can disagree.
rationale: METEOR publishes the national preferred language element with its definition, its ASCL value domain and the explicit note that preference is independent of English fluency. The NACDC data dictionary separately confirms that preferred language is a distinct element from language spoken at home in this holding.
evidence_quote: The language (including sign language) most preferred by the person for communication, as represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Code of language the recipient prefers to speak' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both the definition and the limitation.

value_domain: Australian Standard Classification of Languages (ASCL) language name
value_source: AIHW METEOR data element 659407, 'Person-preferred language, code (ASCL 2016) N[NNN]'
variable_description: The language name that goes with PREFERRED_LANGUAGE_CODE on the same row. It labels the element AIHW METEOR defines as "The language (including sign language) most preferred by the person for communication, as represented by a code", drawn from the ABS Australian Standard Classification of Languages. Alongside COUNTRY_OF_BIRTH_DESC it is what the AIHW uses to describe cultural and linguistic diversity among aged care recipients.
description_source: AIHW METEOR data element 659407, 'Person-preferred language, code (ASCL 2016) N[NNN]'
value_definition: A language name written out. Labels can sit at any level of the ASCL hierarchy, so a value may be a specific language such as Cantonese or a broader group, depending on how the source system recorded it.
limitation: Because labels can come from different levels of the classification, counting distinct text values will treat a broad group and a specific language inside it as two separate languages, which inflates diversity. English also appears here as a genuine preference rather than as a default, so a blank and the value English mean different things and neither should be read as the other.
rationale: METEOR publishes the national preferred language element with its definition and the ASCL value domain, in which the name and the numeric code are two representations of the same classification unit at a stated level.
evidence_quote: The language (including sign language) most preferred by the person for communication, as represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'The person's preferred language as presented by text.' and used one generic sentence for both the value definition and the limitation.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
variable_description: The package level the person actually started on when the home care episode opened. The AIHW defines care level as "The level of care a person receives through an aged care program", and records that home care runs from Level 1 to Level 4, with the earlier CACP, EACH and EACHD packages folded into Level 2 and Level 4 in July 2013. Set it against CARE_APPROVAL_LEVEL on the assessment table, which is what the person was approved for: the difference between the two is the interim package problem, where people take a lower level while waiting for the one they were assessed as needing.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
value_definition: A short text label naming a level. Each level is a funding band with its own daily subsidy, so the value describes the size of the budget attached to the package rather than a measure of the person's need.
limitation: It fixes only the level at the start of the episode. An upgrade partway through does not open a new row, so a long episode recorded at Level 2 can have been delivered mostly at Level 4, and average care level computed from entry values understates what was provided. It is also not comparable across the 2013 transition without mapping the earlier package types.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary carries care level as a data concept of this collection, with the definition and the account of the four home care levels and the earlier package programmes that map onto them.
evidence_quote: The level of care a person receives through an aged care program.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Level of care received on entry' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence as both value definition and limitation.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
variable_description: The day a person started an episode of care with a service, on the home care, residential care and transition care episode tables alike. The AIHW defines the element as "the person's date of entry into a service/facility", and notes that "when used combined with exit_date" it "provides dates for a continuity of service record" - which is what separates it from ADMISSION_DATE on the residential table, where a move between place types inside one home starts a new admission but not a new entry. Everything measured in days for this collection, above all length of stay, is built from this date and EXIT_DATE.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
value_definition: A calendar date in DD/MM/YYYY in the source system, drawn from the payment systems that pay providers for service delivery, so it is the first day of subsidised service rather than a separately recorded arrival.
limitation: Rows are events, not people. The AIHW notes that aged care admissions are counted as entry events rather than as a unique count of people, so someone who leaves home care and comes back has two entry dates. Person-level counts are also broken at the 2013 package transition: recipient identifiers carried over only for people in care at the time, so a person who left CACP, EACH or EACHD and later returned appears as a new recipient.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary documents entry_date and its pairing with exit_date as the continuity of service record, distinguishes it from admission_date, and separately records the identifier break at the August 2013 package transition. The GEN glossary supplies the event-counting convention.
evidence_quote: the person's date of entry into a service/facility, and when used combined with exit_date, provides dates for a continuity of service record
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Date the recipient entered into the program' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both value definition and limitation.

value_domain: aged care programme or care type at entry
value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
variable_description: The kind of care the person began receiving when the episode opened, sitting beside ENTRY_DATE and ENTRY_CARE_LEVEL on the home care episode table. Its main work is to separate the current programme from the ones it replaced: the AIHW records that the Home Care Packages Programme "has been operating since August 2013, when it replaced the earlier aged care packages - Community Aged Care Packages Programme (CACP), Extended Aged Care at Home (EACH) and Extended Aged Care at Home Dementia (EACHD)", so episodes opening before that date carry an earlier programme's care type. Read with ENTRY_CARE_LEVEL it says both what programme and at what level a person entered.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
value_definition: A short text label naming a care or programme type rather than a level. The AIHW does not publish a code list for this column, so the set of labels is best read from the data for the years in scope.
limitation: It cannot distinguish a first entry to aged care from a transfer between providers, since both open a new episode with a new entry type. Nor is it a comparable series across 2013: the same person continuing the same care can carry a legacy package type before the transition and a home care type after it, which will read as a change in care when nothing changed.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary sets out the programme history that this column has to encode, including the August 2013 replacement of CACP, EACH and EACHD by home care packages and the care level mapping that came with it. No published element definition for this column could be verified, so the description is assembled rather than quoted.
evidence_quote: It has been operating since August 2013, when it replaced the earlier aged care packages - Community Aged Care Packages Programme (CACP), Extended Aged Care at Home (EACH) and Extended Aged Care at Home Dementia (EACHD).
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Type of care the recipient received upon entry' and used the generic no-value-list sentence as both value definition and limitation.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
variable_description: The day a person stopped receiving care from a service, closing the episode that ENTRY_DATE opened. The AIHW defines it as "the person's date of exit from a service/facility", which combined with the entry date "provides dates for a continuity of service record". Short absences do not count: the GEN glossary excludes short periods of leave such as family visits or hospital stays, which is why the leave tables hold their own start and end dates. EXIT_REASON on the same row says where the person went.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
value_definition: A calendar date in DD/MM/YYYY in the source system, taken from the provider payment records rather than from a separate departure notice, so it is the last day of subsidised service for the episode.
limitation: An empty exit date is a person still in care at the extract, not an episode with no end, so restricting to completed episodes biases length of stay downwards by dropping the longest current stays. The date is also not a death date even where EXIT_REASON says death, because it records the last day of service rather than a registered date of death.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary documents exit_date and its pairing with entry_date as the continuity of service record for this collection, and the GEN glossary states that exits exclude short periods of leave.
evidence_quote: When a person stops receiving care and support from an aged care service - excluding short periods of leave, such as for family visits or hospital stays.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Date of exit of recipient from a service facility' with the generic no-value-list sentence as both the definition and the limitation.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
variable_description: Where the person went when the episode closed. The AIHW defines the concept as "The reason recorded for discharge from aged care service on separation", adding that these "are effectively the person's destination on separation from aged care", and groups them as hospital, transfer to residential aged care, transfer to community-based care, return to family or home, death, and other. The same column appears on the home care, residential care and transition care episode tables, so it is the field that reveals a pathway: a transition care episode ending in a transfer to residential care is a different outcome from one ending in a return home.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
value_definition: A short text label naming a destination. The source systems behind it use a numbered list that separates hospital, residential aged care at low and high care, death, return to family or home, several return-to-community values distinguished by which programme picks the person up, recipient-initiated and provider-initiated endings, other and a system-generated auto value.
limitation: Death here is a provider-recorded departure reason, not a registered death, so it will not match death registrations and can be coded as other or left as a system-generated value when a claim simply stops. A transfer to another provider inside the same programme also reads as an exit, so counting exits as people leaving aged care will overcount departures from the system.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary carries separation reason as a data concept with the definition and the broad categories, and documents the underlying discharge reason data element with the full list of values commonly in use across the source systems.
evidence_quote: The reason recorded for discharge from aged care service on separation. These are effectively the person's destination on separation from aged care.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's wording about ending the home care episode and the generic no-value-list sentence in both the value definition and the limitation.

value_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Transition Care Program Guidelines (June 2026), section 4.2.1
variable_description: How independent the person was in daily activities when transition care began, scored out of 100. The Transition Care Program guidelines make the measure explicit: "The use of the Modified Barthel Index for assessments by the transition care registered providers at entry to and exit from the TCP is mandatory for Australian Government subsidy payments." That is the baseline against which the whole episode is judged, because transition care exists to restore function after a hospital stay, and the gain to FUNCTIONAL_CAPACITY_EXIT is the programme's central outcome measure.
description_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Transition Care Program Guidelines (June 2026), section 4.2.1
value_definition: An integer from 0 to 100 on the Modified Barthel Index, a ten-item rating of activities of daily living covering feeding, bathing, grooming, dressing, bowel and bladder control, toilet use, transfers, mobility and stairs. Higher scores mean more independence; 0 is complete dependence and 100 is complete independence.
limitation: It is a rating of what the person can do, not of what care they need or receive, so a low score does not establish the intensity of the service delivered. It also cannot be compared with the funding assessments used elsewhere in this collection: the residential care classifications are cost instruments on different scales, and a Modified Barthel score has no crosswalk to them.
rationale: The department's Transition Care Program guidelines state that the Modified Barthel Index is the mandatory entry and exit assessment for transition care providers, which identifies the instrument behind the 0 to 100 score the custodian describes.
evidence_quote: The use of the Modified Barthel Index for assessments by the transition care registered providers at entry to and exit from the TCP is mandatory for Australian Government subsidy payments.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Functional capacity score (between 0-100) of the recipient at time of entry to transition care' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence as both value definition and limitation, without naming the instrument.

value_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Transition Care Program Guidelines (June 2026), section 4.2.1
variable_description: How independent the person was in daily activities when transition care ended, scored out of 100 on the same instrument as the entry score. The Transition Care Program guidelines require it: "The use of the Modified Barthel Index for assessments by the transition care registered providers at entry to and exit from the TCP is mandatory for Australian Government subsidy payments." Subtracting FUNCTIONAL_CAPACITY_ENTRY gives the functional gain over an episode that runs up to 12 weeks, or up to 18 weeks where an extension is granted, and reading that gain against EXIT_REASON separates people who recovered and went home from people who moved on to residential care.
description_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Transition Care Program Guidelines (June 2026), section 4.2.1
value_definition: An integer from 0 to 100 on the Modified Barthel Index, rating ten activities of daily living. It is measured at the close of the transition care episode, so it pairs with the entry score on the same instrument and the same scale.
limitation: A missing exit score is not a zero. Episodes that end with a hospital readmission or a death often have no exit assessment, so dropping blank rows removes the worst outcomes and inflates the average gain. The score also measures independence at one moment at discharge, and says nothing about whether the improvement held once the person was home.
rationale: The department's Transition Care Program guidelines make the Modified Barthel Index the mandatory assessment at both entry to and exit from the programme, which identifies the instrument and the scale behind this column.
evidence_quote: The use of the Modified Barthel Index for assessments by the transition care registered providers at entry to and exit from the TCP is mandatory for Australian Government subsidy payments.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's sentence about the exit score and gave the generic no-value-list sentence as both the value definition and the limitation, without naming the instrument.

value_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Transition Care Program
variable_description: The day the hospital stay began that led to this transition care episode. Transition care exists to help people recover after hospital, and the department's eligibility rule turns on it: to be eligible an older person must "be a patient in a public or private hospital (including Hospital in the Home programs)", must "be ready to be discharged", and must enter transition care within 24 hours of discharge in a residential setting or 48 hours at home. Set against ENTRY_DATE on the same row, the column measures how long the hospital episode ran before transition care picked the person up.
description_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Transition Care Program
value_definition: A calendar date recorded by the transition care provider as part of the referral, not drawn from a hospital data collection.
limitation: It carries no separation date, no diagnosis and no hospital identifier, so it cannot be used as a substitute for admitted patient data or to say what the person was treated for. It also records only the stay that triggered transition care, so a person with several admissions in a year shows just the last one.
rationale: The department publishes the transition care eligibility rule, which fixes the hospital stay as the entry condition for the programme and sets the 24 and 48 hour windows between hospital discharge and transition care entry that this date sits behind. No published element definition for the column could be verified, so the description is assembled.
evidence_quote: To be eligible an older person must: be a patient in a public or private hospital (including Hospital in the Home programs), be ready to be discharged, potentially benefit from accessing a short period of restorative care services.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Date of hospital admission' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence as both the value definition and the limitation.

value_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Managing temporary leave for residential aged care
variable_description: The first day of a break in care that did not end the person's episode. The department describes leave as the situation where a person stops receiving services for a while without giving up their place, and the rules differ by programme: in residential care the reasons are a hospital stay, transition care, social reasons or a declared emergency, while in home care a person can pause for a hospital stay, transition care, residential respite or social reasons. Because a leave row sits inside an episode rather than closing it, subtracting leave days is what turns time enrolled into time actually served.
description_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Managing temporary leave for residential aged care
value_definition: A calendar date. It comes from the monthly claim the provider submits, so it is the first day for which leave rather than ordinary care was claimed.
limitation: It is not an exit and must not be counted as one, or a resident's hospital stay will read as a departure from aged care. The date also carries no destination, so a leave start looks the same whether the person went to hospital, to family or to a respite bed until LEAVE_REASON is read.
rationale: The department publishes what temporary leave is, the leave types available in residential aged care and the requirement that providers record leave dates in the monthly claim, which establishes what this date is and where it comes from. No published element definition for this column could be verified.
evidence_quote: When a resident goes on leave, you must record the leave dates in the monthly claim form you submit to Services Australia.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Start date of leave' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both the value definition and the limitation.

value_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Managing temporary leave for residential aged care
variable_description: The last day of a break in care, closing the period that LEAVE_START_DATE opened. The pair measures how long a resident or home care recipient was away without losing their place, which matters because entitlements are counted in days: residents get unlimited hospital leave but 52 days of social leave in a financial year, and the department states that a person's leave balance resets on 1 July and transfers with them if they change providers. Subtract the two dates to get the days consumed, then read LEAVE_REASON to know which entitlement they came out of.
description_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Managing temporary leave for residential aged care
value_definition: A calendar date taken from the provider's monthly claim. An open value marks leave that had not ended when the extract was taken.
limitation: Days counted from this pair are claimed days, not the person's whereabouts: leave that a provider recorded late or not at all is simply absent, so absence totals built from these rows are a floor. The end date also does not say the person came back, since leave that runs into an exit is closed on the claim rather than on a return.
rationale: The department publishes the leave entitlements measured in days, the annual reset of leave balances and the requirement that providers record leave dates in the monthly claim, which fixes what these dates count and how they are produced. No published element definition for this column could be verified.
evidence_quote: A person's leave balance resets on 1 July each year.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'End date of leave' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence twice.

value_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Managing temporary leave for residential aged care
variable_description: Why the person was away from their aged care service without giving up their place. The department defines the underlying event plainly: "Temporary leave is when a person stops receiving residential care services for a while", and a person "can take leave for any reason" without affecting their right to services. Residential leave types are help with moving in, a hospital stay, transition care, social reasons and emergencies declared by the Australian Government; home care leave covers a hospital stay, transition care, residential respite and other reasons such as social leave. The reason is what decides the entitlement the days come out of and whether the subsidy keeps flowing.
description_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Managing temporary leave for residential aged care
value_definition: A short text label naming a leave type. The categories are administrative rather than clinical: they exist to route the days to the right entitlement, which is why unlimited hospital leave, capped social leave and open-ended transition care leave are separate values.
limitation: It is not a health record. A hospital leave value shows only that the person was in hospital as far as the provider claimed it, with no admission or discharge detail, no diagnosis and no link to hospital data. Social leave is also a residual category covering every reason not separately listed, so it cannot be read as a family visit or a holiday.
rationale: The department publishes what temporary leave is, the complete list of residential leave types and their day entitlements, and the parallel list of reasons a home care participant can pause services, which together are the classification this column encodes.
evidence_quote: Temporary leave is when a person stops receiving residential care services for a while.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the custodian's sentence about temporary leave for residential care and used the generic no-value-list sentence as both the value definition and the limitation.

value_source: Australian Government Department of Veterans' Affairs, Veteran Card
variable_description: Whether the home support client held a Department of Veterans' Affairs treatment card, and which kind. DVA issues three: the "Veteran Card - All Conditions (VCAC) (colloquially known as the Veteran Gold Card) gives access to treatment for all medical conditions", the Specific Conditions or White Card covers accepted service-related conditions and may cover mental health treatment, and the Pharmaceuticals Only or Orange Card gives concessions on prescription medicines and related items. On the home support recipient table the field flags clients who may be getting some of their support from DVA rather than from the Commonwealth Home Support Programme.
description_source: Australian Government Department of Veterans' Affairs, Veteran Card
value_definition: A short text label naming the card held, or its absence. The categories belong to DVA's card scheme rather than to any aged care classification, so they carry the same meaning wherever DVA entitlement is recorded.
limitation: A card holder receiving Veterans' Home Care from DVA has those hours funded and recorded entirely outside this collection, so the home support episodes attached to them understate the support they get. The column is also not a service flag or a veteran flag: it says what treatment the person is entitled to, and a veteran with no accepted condition and no qualifying service holds no card at all.
rationale: DVA publishes the three Veteran Card types with what each entitles the holder to, which is the classification this column records for home support clients.
evidence_quote: Veteran Card - All Conditions (VCAC) (colloquially known as the Veteran Gold Card) gives access to treatment for all medical conditions.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'Whether the person holds a dva entitlement as represented by text.' and used the generic no-value-list sentence for both the definition and the limitation.

value_source: AIHW METEOR data element 270385, 'Person-living arrangement, code N'
variable_description: Whether the person usually lives alone, with family or with other people, recorded at the aged care assessment or on the home support client record. AIHW METEOR defines the national element as "Whether a person usually resides alone or with others, as represented by a code", with the list 1 lives alone, 2 lives with family, 3 lives with others and 9 not stated or inadequately described. In aged care it is one of the strongest predictors on the record of whether someone can be supported at home, because living alone removes the informal care a co-resident partner or child would otherwise supply.
description_source: AIHW METEOR data element 270385, 'Person-living arrangement, code N'
value_definition: A single-digit code or its label, resolving to lives alone, lives with family, lives with others, or a not stated value. The AIHW notes that a separate cohabitation variable on the assessment record captures finer detail, such as living with a spouse, a child or siblings.
limitation: It describes who the person lives with, not what care they get: someone recorded as living with family may have a co-resident who provides nothing, and someone living alone may have a daily visiting carer. The value is also fixed at assessment or at the client record date, so it does not follow a person whose household changes, which in this population happens most often when a partner dies or enters care.
rationale: METEOR publishes the national living arrangement element with the definition and the full code list, and the NACDC data dictionary confirms this holding uses the same values and points to the finer cohabitation variable behind them.
evidence_quote: Whether a person usually resides alone or with others, as represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Identifies the living arrangements of the client.' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence as both the value definition and the limitation.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
variable_description: The postcode of the home support outlet that delivered the service on this row. The AIHW is explicit that geography in this collection follows the provider, not the person: location is "The location where aged care services have been (or can be) delivered, based on the location of the service", derived from the outlet or facility, and "therefore, location does not necessarily reflect where service is provided to a person". OUTLET_STATE and OUTLET_SA2_CODE_2016 beside it are the same outlet at coarser and finer geography, while RECIPIENT_POSTCODE on the client table is the person's own address.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
value_definition: A four-digit Australian postcode as maintained by Australia Post, held against the outlet's physical address. Postcodes are mail delivery areas rather than statistical areas, so they do not nest inside the ABS geography used elsewhere in the collection.
limitation: It is not where the care happened. Home support is delivered in the client's home, and an outlet in one postcode routinely serves several, so mapping service volumes by this column draws the provider network rather than the demand. It also cannot be aggregated cleanly to ABS regions, because postcodes cross statistical area and even state boundaries.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary defines the location concept for this holding, states that it is derived from the location of the service, and warns directly that it does not necessarily reflect where a service was provided to a person.
evidence_quote: Location is based on service delivery location, derived from the location of the service (Home Care outlet or residential aged care facility). Therefore, location does not necessarily reflect where service is provided to a person.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Outlet postcode' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both the value definition and the limitation.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
variable_description: The state or territory of the home support outlet that delivered the service. It is the coarsest of the outlet geography columns on this table, above OUTLET_POSTCODE and OUTLET_SA2_CODE_2016, and it follows the same rule the AIHW sets for the whole collection: location is derived "from the location of the service (Home Care outlet or residential aged care facility)", so it describes the provider rather than the client. Because home support is administered against state and territory funding envelopes, this is the level most published home support totals are broken down at.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, Version 1.0 (2016), cat. no. AGE 80
value_definition: One of the eight Australian states and territories, held as a name or abbreviation for the outlet's physical address. The AIHW lists state and territory as one of the standard structures its location concept can be represented through.
limitation: Cross-border service delivery disappears into it. A client living just over a state line who is served by an outlet on the other side is counted in the outlet's state, which matters most around Albury and Wodonga, the Gold Coast and Tweed, and the Australian Capital Territory and its surrounding New South Wales towns. The column is also not a service location for the visit itself, since the care is delivered at the client's home.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary defines the location concept as service-based, lists state and territory among the structures it is represented through, and warns that it does not necessarily reflect where the service reached the person.
evidence_quote: Location can be represented through various structures, such as: Remoteness structure ... State/territory ... Aged Care Planning Region (ACPR) as defined by DoH ... Statistical Area Level 2 (SA2)

variable_description: The organisation that ran the aged care service, held as a key rather than as a name. It is what groups the many services on aged_service under one owner, and what ties a home support episode back to the body that was paid for it. SERVICE_ID_ENCRYPTED is the finer key: one provider can hold many services.

limitation: It identifies an approved provider, not a corporate group or a brand, so a chain operating under several approvals looks like several unrelated providers, and a merger or a change of approval breaks one operator's history in two. It cannot be matched to the public provider lists or to an ABN either, because the encryption removes everything that could be looked up.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary carries provider as a data concept and provider_id as a common data element, with the definitions, the uniqueness rule, the source-system concatenation behind the raw value and its role as a linking key.
evidence_quote: Unique to each organisation that operates aged care services. The same provider may operate more than one service.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Encrypted provider id' and repeated the generic no-value-list sentence as both the value definition and the limitation.

That last three-way split is what this column isolates: it is the incorporation question, where PROVIDER_ORGANISATION_TYPE on the same row answers the separate question of whether the operator is government, not-for-profit or private.

It also says nothing about ownership or control, so a subsidiary of a large listed group and a stand-alone company can carry the same value.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary documents the provider type data element with its definition, its self-reported context and the code list containing the incorporation categories that this column carries.
evidence_quote: Categorises the provider organisation by type of business.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'The business incorporation type of an aged care provider as represented by text.' and used the generic no-value-list sentence for both the value definition and the limitation.

It is the standard breakdown for almost every published figure about who delivers aged care, and it appears on both the service table and the home support episode table so provision can be split by sector at either level.

The AIHW notes the values are self-described by the organisation and that the source systems hold a longer list, including separate codes for charitable, community-based, religious, local government, state government and territory government, which collapse into the three reported sectors.

A not-for-profit label covers everything from a single small home to a national operator, and the column does not show a service changing hands, since a sale between sectors updates the value with no record that a transfer occurred. Comparing sector shares across years therefore mixes genuine change with recoding.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary carries organisation type as a data concept with the definition and the three-way categorisation, and documents the provider type data element with the full underlying code list and its self-reported basis.
evidence_quote: Type of organisation providing aged care services through a national aged care program.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said 'The business structure type of an aged care provider as represented by text.' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both value definition and limitation.

It sits with PROVIDER_ID_ENCRYPTED, PROVIDER_ORGANISATION_TYPE and PROVIDER_INCORPORATED_BODY, all of which describe the corporate entity rather than the care, and it also appears on the CHSP session table for the grant-funded home support provider. Use it to group providers by home jurisdiction, never to place recipients.

value_definition: Four digits. evidence_quote: The Australian numeric descriptor for a postal delivery area for an address.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried 'not specified' as its value domain and repeated the generic sentence 'The source metadata does not publish a finite value list.' as both its value definition and its limitation, so nothing on the page distinguished a provider address from a service address.

variable_description: The state or territory of the funded organisation's own physical address, held as a name rather than a code. It answers where the provider is based, not where its services operate: a provider headquartered in Victoria can run residential facilities in Queensland and home support outlets in Tasmania, and each of those appears on its own row with its own SERVICE_STATE. On the CHSP session table the same column marks the grant recipient, which matters because home support funding goes to the organisation rather than the person.
