value_definition: A state or territory as text. The AIHW standard code set behind the names covers New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania, Northern Territory, Australian Capital Territory and Other territories, with reserved values for not applicable and not stated. This column holds the name, so the codes themselves do not appear.
limitation: It is the jurisdiction of the organisation's own address, not of the care it funds or delivers. Aggregating recipients or places by provider state will misattribute every service a cross-border provider runs. Because the value is free text rather than a code, spelling and abbreviation can drift between extracts, so grouping on the string is less safe than mapping it to a code first.
rationale: The PLIDA data item list gives the field as the state or territory name for a provider's physical address. METEOR publishes the AIHW's state and territory code set and its labels, and the NACDC user guide establishes the provider-to-service relationship that makes the distinction matter.
evidence_quote: The code set representing Australian states and territories.
supersedes_rationale: The entry restated the data item list wording and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both its value definition and its limitation, leaving a reader unable to tell it apart from SERVICE_STATE.

value_source: AIHW METEOR data element 611398, 'Address—Australian postcode, code (Postcode datafile) NNNN'
variable_description: The postcode recorded against the older person at their aged care assessment, not their address while receiving care. The AIHW warns that address information of this kind "refers to contact information at the time of the person's ACAT assessment, which may not be the same as their usual residence" (National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary). On the CHSP recipient table it carries more weight, because home support is the one aged care program where the NACDC reports geography by the person's home rather than by the outlet, and there it sits beside RECIPIENT_SA2_CODE_2016 and RECIPIENT_STATE as the coarsest of the three.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, version 1.0, 2016
value_definition: Four digits. AIHW METEOR defines the element as "The Australian numeric descriptor for a postal delivery area for an address", format NNNN, with reserved values for not applicable, unknown and not stated.
limitation: It is a point-in-time address that the collection does not update as a person's circumstances change, so it cannot support a mobility measure and it will not show a move into care. For someone in permanent residential care it is a pre-admission address, so it usually differs from where they now live, which is the facility captured by SERVICE_POSTCODE. It is also one postcode per person per extract, so it says nothing about how long they lived there.
rationale: The PLIDA data item list qualifies the field as the recipient's postcode at the time of assessment. The NACDC data dictionary states that recorded recipient addresses are assessment-time contact details rather than usual residence, and its interpretation notes confirm that CHSP is the exception where geography follows the person. METEOR supplies the postcode domain.
evidence_quote: While the ACCR includes address information, this refers to contact information at the time of the person's ACAT assessment, which may not be the same as their usual residence.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Postcode of recipient (at time of assessment)' and gave the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so the assessment-time caveat had no explanation attached to it.

value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS): Volume 1, July 2016, Statistical Area Level 2 (SA2)
variable_description: The small area the Commonwealth Home Support Programme recipient lives in, coded to the ABS 2016 statistical geography. The ABS defines these areas as "medium-sized general purpose areas built up from whole Statistical Areas Level 1" whose "purpose is to represent a community that interacts together socially and economically" (ASGS July 2016). It appears only on the CHSP recipient tables, which is the point: home support is the one aged care program the NACDC geocodes to the person's home instead of to the outlet, so this column and OUTLET_SA2_CODE_2016 on the session table answer different questions — where the person lives against where the service was run from.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS): Volume 1, July 2016, Statistical Area Level 2 (SA2)
value_definition: A nine digit fully hierarchical code made up of the one digit state or territory identifier, the SA4 identifier, the SA3 identifier and a four digit SA2 identifier. The 2016 edition has 2,310 SA2s covering Australia without gaps or overlaps, including 18 non-spatial special purpose codes for migratory, offshore, shipping and no-usual-address records.
limitation: The code is frozen at the 2016 boundaries, so it will not line up with the 2021 SA2s used by the Census products and the newer geography columns elsewhere in PLIDA; joining across editions needs an ABS correspondence and will split or merge populations. It is also the address held for the person in the extract, not an address history, so a person who moved during the 2017 to 2024 window shows one area for the whole period. An SA2 is a statistical area, not a service catchment, so it does not mark which outlets a recipient can reach.
rationale: The variable name pins the ASGS edition, and the ABS publishes the 2016 SA2 definition, code structure and count. The NACDC data dictionary and user guide independently establish that home support is the aged care program whose geography follows the recipient's residential address rather than the service location.
evidence_quote: Statistical Areas Level 2 (SA2) are medium-sized general purpose areas built up from whole Statistical Areas Level 1. Their purpose is to represent a community that interacts together socially and economically.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's sentence about an ASGS identifier and then printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, without saying which edition, what the digits mean, or why a recipient-based geography exists only for home support.

value_source: AIHW METEOR value domain 787653, 'Australian state/territory code N[N]'
variable_description: The state or territory recorded against the older person, taken from the address on file at assessment or registration. It is the coarsest of the recipient geography columns, sitting above RECIPIENT_POSTCODE and, on the CHSP recipient tables, RECIPIENT_SA2_CODE_2016. Whether it tells you anything the service geography does not depends entirely on the program: the AIHW notes that "The location of people using permanent residential care is the same as the service location", while for home care, respite and home support a person can be served from another jurisdiction (National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse: User guide, July 2024).
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse: User guide, July 2024
value_definition: A state or territory as text, drawn from the standard set of the six states, the two internal territories and other territories. The AIHW code set behind those names also reserves values for not applicable and not stated, but this column carries the name rather than the code.
limitation: It is fixed at the time the address was captured, so it will not record an interstate move made during or after entry into care, and it is not the jurisdiction that funded or delivered the care. Aged care programs are Commonwealth funded, so a state here carries no administrative meaning of its own; it is a location, not a payer or a regulator.
rationale: The PLIDA data item list gives the field as the state of the recipient. The NACDC user guide sets out when a recipient's location does and does not coincide with the service's location, which is the only thing that makes this column distinct from SERVICE_STATE. METEOR supplies the state and territory value set.
evidence_quote: The location of people using permanent residential care is the same as the service location. For other aged care programs, however, people may receive care from services in different locations.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the four-word custodian description 'State of recipient' and the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it read as interchangeable with SERVICE_STATE and PROVIDER_STATE.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse: User guide, July 2024
variable_description: The date this copy of the table is current to, which makes it the vintage stamp rather than anything about a person or a service. It is constant across every row of a table and matches the table's own suffix, so it is what separates the jun2024, oct2024, jan2025, apr2025 and jun2025 cuts of the same aged care collection. That matters because the AIHW refreshes history at every supply: "Each annual supply also refreshes data from previous years where records have been revised or updated" (National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse: User guide, July 2024), so one episode can appear in several vintages with different values, and this column is how you choose which one you are reading.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse: User guide, July 2024
value_definition: A single calendar date, identical on every row of a table. NACDC dates are held in day, month and year form. The value tracks the extract cycle rather than a fixed reporting calendar, so it takes a small number of distinct values across the whole dataset — one per supply.
limitation: It is not the date of any event. It does not say when care was given, when a person was assessed, when an approval started or when a record was created; ENTRY_DATE, EXIT_DATE, ADMISSION_DATE, APPROVAL_START_DATE and SESSION_CONDUCTED_DATE do that. Nor does it guarantee completeness up to that date: aged care activity is reported with a lag, so late records for a period appear only in the next vintage, and an activity count taken from an early extract will be biased down near its own reference date.
rationale: The custodian's own wording defines the field as the latest date for which data in the table is available, updated with each supply. The NACDC user guide documents the supply cycle and the refresh of prior years that gives the column its purpose, and the PLIDA table names carry the matching extract dates.
evidence_quote: Unit record data from the Aged Care Data Warehouse are typically supplied to the AIHW in September each year for aged care program activity up to 30 June of that year. Each annual supply also refreshes data from previous years where records have been revised or updated.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's sentence and gave the generic no-value-list line as both value definition and limitation, so a reader had no way to know the column is a vintage marker and not an event date.

value_source: AIHW GEN Aged Care Data, Providers of aged care
variable_description: The kind of care this outlet or facility holds an approval to provide, which is what separates a residential aged care home from a home care outlet or a transition care service in a table that calls them all services. It effectively predicts which episode table the row's SERVICE_ID_ENCRYPTED will turn up in: rac_episode for residential, hcp_episode for home care, tcp_episode for transition care. Read it with SERVICE_TYPE, which names the broader program, and with SERVICE_STATUS, which says whether the service was operating at REFERENCE_DATE.
description_source: AIHW GEN Aged Care Data, Providers of aged care
value_definition: Text names for the care types funded under the Aged Care Act 1997 and the flexible programs beside it. AIHW GEN reports services by care type across permanent residential care, residential respite care, home care packages, transition care, short-term restorative care, the Multi-Purpose Services Program, the Innovative Care Programme and the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Flexible Aged Care Program.
limitation: An approval is a permission, not activity: a service approved for a care type may have taken no recipients in the period, and the column carries no dates so it cannot show when an approval was granted or withdrawn. It is also about the service, not the person, so it must not be confused with CARE_APPROVAL_TYPE and CARE_APPROVAL_LEVEL on the assessment table, which record what an individual was assessed as eligible for. Home support sits outside this frame entirely, because CHSP providers hold grant agreements rather than care type approvals and their activity is recorded on the separate chsp tables.
rationale: The custodian defines the field as the type of care the service is approved for. AIHW GEN publishes the care types by which aged care services are counted, and the NACDC user guide explains the funding difference that keeps home support out of the approval framework. The mapping from care type to episode table follows from the registry's own table layout.
evidence_quote: A service can be a facility that provides aged care (such as home care or residential care). A service can also be an outlet that provides home support.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's sentence and gave the generic no-value-list line twice, so it neither named a single care type nor distinguished a service's approval from a person's approval.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, version 1.0, 2016
variable_description: The individual aged care outlet or facility, as an encrypted key that is "unique to each aged care service" (National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary). It is the join that turns an episode into a place: aged_service holds the outlet's address, approvals, status and size, while rac_episode, hcp_episode and tcp_episode carry the same key against each person's admission and discharge. PROVIDER_ID_ENCRYPTED sits one level above it, because one provider runs many services. The CHSP tables deliberately do not carry it — home support comes from a different source system, so its outlets are identified by the provider key and the OUTLET_POSTCODE, OUTLET_STATE and OUTLET_SA2_CODE_2016 columns instead.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, version 1.0, 2016
value_definition: An opaque encrypted string. In the source collection the service identifier is alphanumeric and of various lengths, formed by concatenating a source system prefix with a unique service identifier; encryption removes that structure, so the value cannot be decoded, cannot be matched to a named facility in published aged care listings, and is useful only for joining one record to another.
limitation: It identifies a service as an administrative entity, not a building or a business. A facility that changes hands, is re-approved or is restructured can be issued a new identifier, which breaks one continuous site history into two and can look like a closure followed by an opening. The reverse also happens: a single identifier can cover a facility that was rebuilt or relocated. Because the key originates in the aged care payment systems, it will not match the Data Exchange outlet identifiers behind the CHSP tables, so home support and residential care activity cannot be joined at the outlet level.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary defines the service identifier, its uniqueness and its composition, and the user guide explains that the aged care payment systems and the Data Exchange use different service identifiers. The registry's own table layout shows the key present on aged_service and the residential, home care and transition care episode tables but absent from the CHSP tables.
evidence_quote: Unique to each aged care service.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Encrypted service id' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both its value definition and its limitation, so nothing said what the key joins or where it stops working.

value_source: AIHW METEOR data element 611398, 'Address—Australian postcode, code (Postcode datafile) NNNN'
variable_description: The postcode of the aged care facility or outlet itself, and for most NACDC reporting this is the geography that gets used. SERVICE_STATE, SERVICE_SA2_CODE and SERVICE_SA2_NAME on the same row are the same address at coarser and finer resolutions, so this is the level at which two facilities in one SA2 stay distinguishable. Whether it also locates the people is a question of program: the AIHW states that "The location of people using permanent residential care is the same as the service location. For other aged care programs, however, people may receive care from services in different locations" (National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse: User guide, July 2024).
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse: User guide, July 2024
value_definition: Four digits. AIHW METEOR defines the element as "The Australian numeric descriptor for a postal delivery area for an address", format NNNN, with reserved values for not applicable, unknown and not stated.
limitation: For home care, respite and home support this is where the service is administered, not where the care happens, so mapping recipients to it will overstate demand near outlets and understate it in the areas they drive to. It is a single postcode for a service that may cover a whole region, and it gives no radius, no boundary and no measure of how far people travel. Postcode areas are also mail rounds, so they do not nest inside the SA2 in the next column.
rationale: The custodian gives the field as the postcode of a service's physical address. METEOR publishes the postcode domain, and the NACDC user guide and data dictionary both state that NACDC geography is based on the service location except for home support, and that the person's location matches the service's only for permanent residential care.
evidence_quote: The location of people using permanent residential care is the same as the service location. For other aged care programs, however, people may receive care from services in different locations.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Postcode of physical address of a service' and printed the generic no-value-list line twice, so it did not warn that this is the default geography of NACDC reporting and is not the recipient's location.

value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Statistical Area Level 2
variable_description: The small statistical area containing the aged care facility or outlet, which is the unit AIHW aged care reporting uses to compare service supply across the country. SERVICE_SA2_NAME on the same row is the label for this code and carries no extra information. Because the NACDC geocodes most programs by service location rather than recipient location, this is the column that drives supply-side measures such as places per head of older population, while RECIPIENT_SA2_CODE_2016 on the CHSP recipient tables is the only demand-side equivalent in the dataset.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Statistical Area Level 2
value_definition: A nine digit fully hierarchical code: one digit for the state or territory, then the SA4, SA3 and four digit SA2 identifiers. The ABS defines the areas themselves as "medium-sized general purpose areas built up from whole Statistical Areas Level 1" that "represent a community that interacts together socially and economically".
limitation: The ASGS edition is not stated in the metadata, unlike RECIPIENT_SA2_CODE_2016 on the CHSP tables, so the codes cannot safely be assumed to match those and should be checked against a boundary file before any join to Census or population denominators. Beyond that, an SA2 is not a catchment: a residential facility draws residents from well beyond its own area, and a home care outlet's clients are scattered across many SA2s, so a count of services by SA2 measures where providers are registered, not where care is consumed.
rationale: The custodian defines the field as the ASGS SA2 identifier for a service's physical address, and the ABS publishes the SA2 definition and the nine digit code structure. The edition is left medium confidence because the metadata names no edition year, in contrast with the recipient SA2 column.
evidence_quote: An SA2 is identifiable by a 9-digit fully hierarchical code comprising the 1-digit State or Territory identifier, and Statistical Areas Level 2-4 identifiers.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's sentence about an ASGS identifier and gave the generic no-value-list line as both definition and limitation, without saying what the digits mean or that the edition is unstated.

value_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Statistical Area Level 2
variable_description: The readable label for the statistical area holding the aged care facility or outlet, and the same fact as SERVICE_SA2_CODE beside it. Its only advantage is that it needs no lookup, which is why it is worth using for a table heading or a map label and not for a join. The area it names is a community-sized ABS region built from whole SA1s, so it usually reads like a suburb or a group of suburbs even though it is neither.
description_source: ABS, Australian Statistical Geography Standard (ASGS) Edition 3, Statistical Area Level 2
value_definition: The ABS name of an SA2, as text. Names are assigned to the areas of the main ASGS structure, in which the ABS builds SA2s from whole SA1s to "represent a community that interacts together socially and economically".
limitation: Never treat the name as a stable key. SA2s are redrawn between ASGS editions and names are added, retired and reused, so joining datasets on the text will silently drop rows and merge areas that are not the same; the code column, with a known edition, is the safe key. The name also encourages a second error — reading an SA2 as a suburb. It is a statistical area that frequently spans several suburbs or splits one, so it will not agree with a suburb-level address list.
rationale: The custodian defines the field as the ASGS SA2 identifier for the service's physical address represented as text, which makes it the label for the code in the neighbouring column. The ABS publishes what an SA2 is and how the areas are built, which is what determines how the name should and should not be used.
evidence_quote: Statistical Areas Level 2 (SA2s) are medium-sized general purpose areas built up from whole Statistical Areas Level 1 (SA1s). Their purpose is to represent a community that interacts together socially and economically.
supersedes_rationale: The entry restated the custodian's sentence and printed the generic no-value-list line twice, so it read identically to SERVICE_SA2_CODE and gave no reason to prefer one over the other.

variable_description: The state or territory in which the aged care facility or outlet physically sits, as a name rather than a code. It is the level at which most published aged care supply figures are broken down, and it is unaffected by ASGS boundary changes, unlike the SA2 columns on the same row, so it is the safest way to group services over a long run of extracts. It can differ from PROVIDER_STATE on the same row whenever a provider operates across borders.

value_definition: A state or territory as text, from the standard set of the six states, the two internal territories and other territories. The AIHW code set behind those names reserves further values for not applicable and not stated; this column holds the name only.
limitation: Aged care is Commonwealth funded, so the state here is a location and not a funder, a regulator or a policy boundary; state differences in this dataset reflect where facilities were built, not different programmes. For home care and home support it is also the state the service is run from rather than the state a recipient lives in, so it cannot stand in for RECIPIENT_STATE except in permanent residential care.
rationale: The custodian gives the field as the state or territory name for a service's physical address. METEOR publishes the standard state and territory value set, and the NACDC user guide sets out that service location and recipient location coincide only for permanent residential care.
evidence_quote: The code set representing Australian states and territories.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'State or territory name for the physical address of a service' and gave the generic no-value-list sentence as both definition and limitation, leaving it indistinguishable from PROVIDER_STATE and RECIPIENT_STATE.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, version 1.0, 2016
variable_description: Whether the outlet or facility was actually operating as at REFERENCE_DATE, as against approved but not yet open, or closed. The AIHW defines the underlying concept as "The operational status of places, services and providers" and notes that "While other codes for status exist in source data, NACDC commonly only reports on operational places, services or providers" (National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary), so in a NACDC extract this column is close to constant and its real job is to let you drop the services that were never open. Read it with SERVICE_TOTAL_PLACES, since only an operating service has operational places behind that count.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, version 1.0, 2016
value_definition: Short status labels as text, derived in the source systems from a service status code. The parallel place-level concept in NACDC divides allocations into operational places, unused or offline places and provisionally allocated places, and the service-level status is the same idea applied to the whole outlet.
limitation: It is a status at one instant, not a history, so it cannot date an opening or a closure; a facility that shut halfway through the year still shows a single value in the extract, and only the gap in the episode tables reveals when it stopped taking residents. It is also not a quality signal: it says the service is operating, not that it is accredited, compliant or performing, and none of the sanction and accreditation information published elsewhere by the regulator is in this column.
rationale: The custodian defines the field as the operational status of the service in text. The NACDC data dictionary defines the status concept, names the service status code it derives from, and states that NACDC reporting normally retains only operational units, which explains the column's low variation. The user guide supplies the place-level status categories that the service-level status parallels.
evidence_quote: While other codes for status exist in source data, NACDC commonly only reports on operational places, services or providers.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's sentence and printed the generic no-value-list line twice, so a reader could not tell that the column is near-constant by design or that it says nothing about accreditation.

value_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Commonwealth Home Support Program (CHSP) Service List Mapping Guide, June 2025
variable_description: The finest description of what was actually delivered at a home support session: podiatry rather than allied health, garden maintenance rather than home maintenance, visiting rather than social support. It is the third level of the Commonwealth Home Support Programme service list that ran until 30 June 2025, sitting under SERVICE_TYPE_DESC and SERVICE_TYPE_CODE on the same row. Since the chsp_episode tables cover 2017 to 2024, every value here belongs to that old list, which the Department rebuilt for the Aged Care Act 2024.
description_source: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Commonwealth Home Support Program (CHSP) Service List Mapping Guide, June 2025
value_definition: Text names from the pre-1 July 2025 CHSP service sub-type list, which sat beneath a service type, which in turn sat beneath one of three services — community and home support, assistance with care and housing, and care relationships and carer support. Examples run from podiatry, physiotherapy and exercise physiology under allied health and therapy services, through garden maintenance and minor home maintenance and repairs, to direct and indirect transport.
limitation: The sub-type detail is uneven and cannot be treated as a clean taxonomy. Several service types carried catch-all sub-types such as other allied health and therapy services and other goods and equipment, which the Department retired in 2025 and replaced with a requirement that providers report the actual service delivered, so a sub-type distribution understates specific services and overstates residual ones. Values also do not map one-to-one onto the post-2025 service names, so a time series that crosses 1 July 2025 needs the Department's mapping tables rather than a string match.
rationale: The Department's mapping guide sets out the CHSP service list as service, service type and service sub-type before 1 July 2025, and enumerates the sub-types for each service type, which is the vocabulary this column draws on for the 2017 to 2024 tables. Rated medium because the guide documents the programme's list rather than the NACDC column itself.
evidence_quote: This appendix maps the old (pre-1 July 2025) service list to the CHSP service list effective from 1 July 2025.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated 'Type of home support service (service subtype) as represented by text' and gave the generic no-value-list line twice, so it named no sub-type and did not warn that the classification was replaced in 2025.

value_domain: count of allocated aged care places (integer)
value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, version 1.0, 2016
variable_description: How big the service is, measured in government-funded places — beds in a residential facility, packages in a home care outlet — as at 30 June of the previous financial year. The AIHW defines the size of a service as "the number of operational places available through the outlet/facility" (National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary), and this is the standard size measure in aged care reporting, used to build supply ratios against the older population of SERVICE_SA2_CODE. It is capacity, and the episode tables are the only place to find out whether that capacity was used.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, version 1.0, 2016
value_definition: A whole number of places. Places are the packages or beds allocated to a service or provider and are the standard measure of system capacity; an allocation is made up of operational places, unused or offline places and provisionally allocated places, and this count is the operational allocation as at the previous 30 June.
limitation: It is capacity, not occupancy, and service-level occupancy rates are not published, so a large number here does not mean a large caseload. It is also blind to composition: residential places do not distinguish permanent from respite, and have not distinguished low from high care since 1 July 2014. The gap that catches people out is home care — places have not been reportable for the Home Care Packages Program since 27 February 2017, because funding follows the recipient rather than the outlet, so a busy home care service can show no places at all. Finally the figure is an as-at-30-June value for the previous financial year while the rest of the row is current to REFERENCE_DATE, so the two are not aligned in time.
rationale: The custodian defines the field as the number of aged care places applied to the service for the previous financial year as at 30 June. The NACDC data dictionary defines size of service in terms of operational places, and the user guide sets out the place status categories and the 2014 and 2017 changes that limit what the count covers.
evidence_quote: The size of the service outlet or residential aged care facility, calculated by the number of operational places available through the outlet/facility.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's sentence and printed the generic no-value-list line as both value definition and limitation, so it did not warn that the count is capacity rather than use, or that home care outlets have carried no places since 2017.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, version 1.0, 2016
variable_description: The aged care programme the service operates under. The AIHW defines the matching concept as the "Type of aged care program", derived from the service type code and "broadly categorised as: Residential, Community, Transition Care" (National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary). Treat the description carried in the PLIDA data item list with suspicion: it defines a child care service and has been mapped onto this column by mistake, so nothing in it applies to aged care. The column pairs with SERVICE_APPROVAL_CARE_TYPE, which is the specific care type the service is approved to deliver, and it is the field the NACDC derives its published programme type from.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse Data Dictionary, version 1.0, 2016
value_definition: Text programme labels. The AIHW's programme type concept, which it derives from the service type code, is "broadly categorised as: Residential, Community, Transition Care", and the modern programme set in the NACDC covers home support, home care, residential care, flexible care and aged care eligibility assessments.
limitation: It is the programme a service is funded under, not the mix of care it delivers, and it does not give a care level — Home Care Package levels 1 to 4 and the AN-ACC classifications live with the person, not the service. Because each programme's outlet is a separate service row, this column cannot identify an organisation that spans programmes; PROVIDER_ID_ENCRYPTED does that. Its greatest risk is the wrong description shipped alongside it, which invites a reader to interpret aged care rows as child care.
rationale: The NACDC data dictionary defines programme type and states that it is derived from the service type code, which places this column at the programme level, and the user guide enumerates the current programme set. Rated medium because the custodian's own description for this field is a mis-mapped child care definition and gives no support.
evidence_quote: Program type ... Type of aged care program. ... Related data item(s): Derived from 'Service type code'.
supersedes_rationale: The entry carried the mis-mapped child care description as its only text and printed the generic no-value-list line twice, so the page asserted something false about an aged care column.

value_source: AIHW GEN Aged Care Data, Fact sheet 2023-24 Commonwealth Home Support Programme (CHSP)
variable_description: The category of home support delivered at the session — domestic assistance, allied health and therapy services, transport, home maintenance, nursing, meals or social support. It is the label that defines the session itself, because the AIHW records CHSP activity so that "A session represents the services provided to one or more people by a service outlet, for a particular day and a particular service type" (National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse: User guide, July 2024). SERVICE_TYPE_CODE on the same row is the coded form of this value and SERVICE_SUBTYPE_DESC breaks it down further, so a person receiving three kinds of help in a week appears on three rows.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse: User guide, July 2024
value_definition: Text names from the Commonwealth Home Support Programme service type list in force before 1 July 2025. AIHW GEN reporting for 2023–24 shows the scale of the common ones: domestic assistance reached 40% of recipients, allied health and therapy services 31%, transport 20%, home maintenance 19% and individual social support 15%.
limitation: It labels a session, not a person's care. A count of rows by service type counts deliveries by outlets, not older people, and a person who receives a service every week outweighs one who receives it once. It also says nothing about need: home support is delivered against what a provider is funded and able to offer, so the absence of nursing on a person's rows does not mean nursing was not needed, only that this outlet did not deliver it under that label.
rationale: The NACDC user guide states that a CHSP session is defined by a service outlet, a day and a service type, which is exactly the grain of the chsp_episode table and its SESSION_CONDUCTED_DATE, SERVICE_TYPE_CODE and SERVICE_TYPE_DESC columns. The AIHW GEN CHSP fact sheet names the service types and their shares of recipients.
evidence_quote: A session represents the services provided to one or more people by a service outlet, for a particular day and a particular service type.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Description for type of service' and gave the generic no-value-list sentence twice, so it named no service type and did not explain that the value defines the session.

value_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse: User guide, July 2024
variable_description: The day the home support session took place, and the only event date on a CHSP row. Home support is recorded differently from the rest of aged care: "CHSP episodes are collected per provision of service, or 'session', while home care, residential care and flexible care episodes are collected per entry into care, or 'admission'" (National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse: User guide, July 2024), so where rac_episode and hcp_episode have entry and exit dates, this table has one date per delivery. Combined with SERVICE_TYPE_DESC it builds a person's pattern of home support across a year, and it is the only way to see frequency or gaps.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse: User guide, July 2024
value_definition: A calendar date, held in the NACDC's day, month and year form. One value per session row, so a recipient has as many dates in a year as they had deliveries, across as many service types as they used.
limitation: A session date is not a person's episode of care, and the row it sits on may cover several people at once. The AIHW warns that multiple recipients can attend a single session, that the data are not captured at a person level, and that the volume of services received by an individual recipient therefore cannot be calculated — so the minutes, quantity and cost columns beside this date belong to the session, not to the recipient. CHSP also has no entry or exit dates, so a person's start and end of home support has to be inferred from the first and last session date, and a long gap cannot be distinguished from a break in reporting.
rationale: The NACDC user guide defines the CHSP session, states that CHSP episodes are collected per provision of service rather than per admission, and sets out the person-level limits of session data. The registry's own layout confirms the grain: this table carries a session date, service type and cost but no entry, exit or admission dates.
evidence_quote: Multiple recipients can attend a single session and these data are not captured at a person-level. It is possible to calculate the number of services provided against each session, but it is not possible to calculate the volume of services received by individual recipients.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Date session was conducted' and printed the generic no-value-list line twice, so it never explained what a session is or why CHSP has no admission dates.

value_source: AIHW METEOR data element 287316, 'Person—sex, code N'
variable_description: The recipient's sex as a single digit, following the AIHW standard element that defines it as "The biological distinction between male and female, as represented by a code" (METEOR data element 287316). In this dataset it is the value the aged care payment or assessment system already held, not something the person confirmed for the collection, and the AIHW's own guidance is candid about what that means: "It is not known if the people completing these records interpreted sex to mean sex at birth or gender identity". SEX_DESC on the same row is the text label for the same value, so the pair carries one fact twice.
description_source: AIHW METEOR data element 287316, 'Person—sex, code N'
value_definition: A single digit on the AIHW standard: 1 male, 2 female, 3 intersex or indeterminate, with 9 for not stated or inadequately described. The aged care collections record male or female for almost every recipient.
limitation: It is not gender, and the two are collected separately in aged care: the National Screening and Assessment Form used by My Aged Care records a person's gender rather than sex, so a recipient's value here need not agree with their assessment record. The intersex or indeterminate category is also effectively unusable — the AIHW does not typically report results for people whose sex is recorded as another term because the numbers are too small — so a count from this column will look like a clean binary even where the underlying records are not.
rationale: The custodian defines the field as the sex of the person represented by a code, which is the AIHW standard element published in METEOR with its permissible values. The NACDC user guide describes how sex is actually captured in aged care systems and what the AIHW will and will not report from it.
evidence_quote: The biological distinction between male and female, as represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's sentence and printed the generic no-value-list line as both definition and limitation, despite METEOR publishing the exact code set and the NACDC user guide publishing the caveats.

value_source: AIHW METEOR data element 287316, 'Person—sex, code N'
variable_description: The written-out form of the recipient's sex, holding the same fact as SEX_CODE beside it. It exists so a table can be read without a code lookup, and it is the safer of the two to display and the less safe of the two to group by. Like the code, it comes from whatever the aged care payment or assessment system held for the person rather than from a question asked for this collection.
description_source: AIHW METEOR data element 287316, 'Person—sex, code N'
value_definition: Short text labels matching the AIHW standard categories of male, female and intersex or indeterminate, with a not stated category for missing values. The underlying standard is the same one behind SEX_CODE.
limitation: Label text is not guaranteed to be stable, so male, Male and M can all appear across extracts and programmes, and grouping on the string rather than the code can split one category into several. It is also worth remembering what the label does not carry: it is a recorded sex, not a self-reported gender, and the AIHW notes that most aged care reporting translates it into the words men and women even though some recipients will not identify with those terms.
rationale: The custodian defines the field as the sex of the person represented by text, which is the label form of the code element published in METEOR. The NACDC user guide describes how sex is recorded in aged care systems and how the AIHW reports it. Rated medium because the exact label strings used in the PLIDA extract are not published.
evidence_quote: The biological distinction between male and female, as represented by a code.
supersedes_rationale: The entry repeated the custodian's sentence and gave the generic no-value-list line twice, so it read identically to SEX_CODE and offered no reason to choose between them.

value_source: ABS, Person Level Integrated Data Asset (PLIDA)
variable_description: The older person, as the de-identified person key that ties every aged care table together and out to the rest of PLIDA. It is what lets a recipient's demographics on aged_recipient join to their eligibility assessment on hcp_assessment, their admissions on rac_episode, hcp_episode and tcp_episode, their leave on rac_leave and hcp_leave, and their home support sessions on the chsp tables — and then, through the ABS Person Linkage Spine, to Medicare, PBS, income support and death registrations. That single key is an achievement rather than a given: inside the source collection the aged care programmes use different person identifiers, so it is the product of AIHW record linkage.
description_source: AIHW, National Aged Care Data Clearinghouse: User guide, July 2024
value_definition: An opaque de-identified person identifier issued for the supplying agency's PLIDA holdings, unique to a person within them and joined to the ABS Person Linkage Spine through the agency spine file. The value carries no name, date of birth or address, has no internal structure, and cannot be decoded or matched against any published aged care record, so there is no finite list.
limitation: The key is only as good as the linkage behind it, and coverage is not uniform across the aged care programmes it spans. Home support is the weakest: the AIHW expects CHSP providers to report no more than 5% of their clients as unidentified in each reporting period, so an unlinked person can be missing from the chsp tables while present in residential care. The key is also a person and not an episode or a household — repeated values are repeated dealings with the aged care system, not repeated people — and it will not join to the Aged Care Management Payment System or Data Exchange identifiers used in published aged care statistics.
rationale: The custodian gives the field as the person identifier for the integrated asset, and the ABS publishes how PLIDA links agency datasets through the Person Linkage Spine. The NACDC user guide documents that aged care programmes carry different person identifiers requiring linkage, and gives the reporting expectation that bounds home support identification.
evidence_quote: CHSP providers are expected to report no more than 5% of their clients as unidentified in each reporting period.
supersedes_rationale: The entry said only 'Synthetic MADIP Person ID' and printed the generic no-value-list sentence as both its definition and its limitation, so it did not say which tables the key joins, that it reaches the spine, or where the linkage is weakest.
